speechtext: of the Intercolonial railway, and of the engineers of the Government railway service that the interests of the country, the interests of New Brunswick, the interests of St. John, and the interests of the Government railways will be much better served by having the railway on the west side into St. John as set forth in the legislation now suggested by the Acting Minister of Railways. Having discussed this matter fully with those gentlemen, having endeavoured to view it entirely from the standpoint of the public interest, of the province, and of the city which I represent, I have come to the same conclusion, and I feel that it is my duty to state here that I heartily concur in the conclusion to which they have come. A little later, I think we will see, as has been indicated by the general manager of the Government railways, a railway connection between this railway and the systems of the United States; that the Government of Canada will build a road from a point somewhere between Fredericton and Andover connecting with the Maine Central railway so that the products of the Intercolonial and of the government railways in Northern and central New Brunswick may have an independent outlet to the United States. This I believe w'ill be of tremendous advantage to the Intercolonial and to the government railway systems, particularly so far as the lumber business of the country is concerned. The general manager of the Intercolonial does not hesitate to express the opinion that a line of railway running from the St. John Valley railway and connecting in the State of Maine with the American system of railways will be a mokt profitable piece of railway to all the government railways in the northern and central parts of New Brunswick, and an advantage to St. John. An independent connection with the railway systems of the United States, in addition to the connection which it has now, will, I think, be one of the great advantages that will flow from the legislation which is now proposed by the Acting Minister of Railways. I say once more, Mr. Chairman, and I am speaking to-day because I may not be here when the Bill comes up, and I do not wish my absence to be misunderstood in any way, that the measure before the House has my full concurrence. I think it is very much in the interests of the province from which I come.

It is not my intention to discuss this question because it relates to a part of the province in which I am not specially interested, and does not relate to my own particular constituency. But I would like to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries if he has any information as to the cost of the road, if it is built from Westfield to St, John, and as to how it will compare with the cost of the connection originally proposed on the east side of the river.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mile for mile, I think it
would cost about the same to build the railway on the east side as on the west side. But on the east side there was a tunnel after the railway left the bridge across the river that would have been a very expensive piece of work. I believe that the cost of construction of the road- it has been well constructed, being laid with heavy rails-has been, about $37,000 per mile as against about $72,000 per mile in the case of the Transcontinental through the province of New Brunswick. From Westfield into the city of St. John I presume that the cost, mile for mile, will be pretty much the same as from Woodstock to Fredericton and from Fredericton to Gagetown.

I would ask the Minister of Railways if this part of the road is built from Westfield to St. John and on to Courtenay Bay, is it the intention that it should be built toy this Government or by the Provincial Government or toy the iSt. John and Quebec Railway Company under the bond guarantee?	.

The arrangement we are entering into is an arrangement between the New Brunswick Government and the Dominion Government, so far as the railway to Westfield is concerned only. If at any future time the matter is taken up, the Dominion Government will build if the New Brunswick Government still desires; but if the New Brunswick Government thinks it is of any advantage to continue this road, we have no objection.

I understand the minister to say that if the road is built from a point at or near Westfield it will be by the St. John and Quebec railway under the bond guarantee by the Provincial Government, to connect with the Canadian Pacific railway.

I understand that, if this
Government undertakes to get running rights over the Canadian Pacific into St. John, but if they fail to get running rights, he has guaranteed this committee that they are going to build a line from Westfield into St. John. Is that a guarantee coming from this Government to build that road, or will there be further responsibility put upon the shoulders of the people of New Brunswick?

This Bill provides that this
railway company shall acquire running rights between Westfield and St. John. If they cannot do so, this Government will acquire running rights over the Canadian Pacific into St. John and to the terminals. This agreement is only to Westfield. From that on, if it is necessary, or if we cannot get running rights that are satisfactory, the Dominion Government will build a road from Westfield into St. John.

I have listened with
close attention to the discussion of this resolution. I am not so much interested in the terminus at St. John as I am in the towns of Andover and Grand Falls. These two towns are situated in my constituency and on behalf of the people of the St. John valley, I feel very much disappointed with the proposal which is now before this committee. I read in this resolution:
That upon the completion of the line from Gagetown to Westfield the Dominion will enter into a lease thereof and operate the same pending the completion of the remaining line to Andover, all in accordance with terms and conditions to be agreed upon in each case, including the 40 and 60 per cent division of gross earnings hereinafter referred to.
I understand that under this resolution, the railway will only be built as far as Andover. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) said that there is no necessity for the present to build a line from Andover to Grand Falls. I see by this resolution that there is an estimate for the building of a line from Andover to Centreville, a distance of 26 miles, and I see also by the resolution that this part of the railway will not be built for some time. I would like to ask the Acting Minister of Railways if it is the intention to build that line from Centreville to Andover this year, or next year?

I may say for the information of the hon. member (Mr. Michaud) that this Bill will provide that we shall take over each part of the road as it is completed under a temporary lease, which
will continue until the whole road is completed, when we will take a 99 year lease of the whole system. 'They have now completed the road, as I understand, from Centreville to Gagetown. We are operating that under a temporary lease. When they get to Westfield we will take a 99-year lease, or another temporary lease, until they build to Andover. The Bill gives the railway company a certain length of time to build the road between Centreville and Andover, as it does between Gagetown and Westfield. We cannot force them to start, or -complete, the road until that time has lapsed. We have urged and insisted that the railway company shall get connection between Westfield and Gagetown at once, or within -the next few months, in order that we can operate this line between St. John and the west by connection with the Transcontinental railway. The other road, between Centreville and AndoveT, we would like to see built as soon as the company can do so, but that is a matter that *rests with the company. They must build the road as soon as they can, or at least within the time we have given them under this agreement. The hon. gentleman has spoken about the connection between Grand Falls and Andover. I feel myself that it is not necessary to construct 5 p.m. that -road now in so far as the Government railway system is concerned-. The operating of two railways side by side for 25 miles would mean an extra expense, to say nothing of the extra cost of building the line. People can, get from St. John to Grand Falls, if they so desire, by simply transferring at Andover to the Canadian Pacific. As has been stated by my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen), now is the time to get running rights between Andover and Grand Falls, and thus save the expense of paralleling that line. We do not desire to do any injustice to- that section of the country. I would not favour the building of a line between Andover and Grand Falls, knowing that they already have a -railway from Andover to Grand Falls, and that this would simply be paralleling the existing line for that distance. We all believe that the time has come when we should not parallel any more railways than we can absolutely help. We can perform this service by getting running rights over the - existing railway.

I am sorry to hear from the Acting Minister of Railways that he does not see his way clear to build the railway from Andover to Grand Falls. I

am afraid the railway will never be built from Centreville to Andover. It was understood a few years ago that a railway was to built from Andover to Grand Falls, but from what I can gather from the remarks of my hon. friend, we are not going to h?ve that part of the line built. It was the policy of the Provincial Government to build that road from St. John to Centreville, and from there to branch out in the other direction instead of going by Grand Falls. From the observations of my hon. friend, we have reason to believe that this will be done. The people of Grand Falls have been promised by the Premier of our province that this line, in order to be completed, had to be constructed from St. John all through the St. John valley and as far up as Grand Falls. The town of Grand Falls supplies such an amount of freight each year as in the long run would make profitable a railway from Centreville to that point. I was rather amazed at the remarks of my hon. friend when he spoke about that branch from McGivney junction to Fredericton. He says that there is quite a grade and that they can haul a pretty big load because the grade is from Me-Givney junction down to Fredericton. In that connection he speaks of securing the right to rum trains over the Canadian Pacific from Grand Falls to Andover and then from Westfield to St. John. From his remarks I gather that this St. John Valley railway will not, after all, be much of a railway. They aie to secure running rights over a part of the Canadian Pacific, Tunning rights over a part of the Intercolonial, and then running rights over the Canadian Pacific from Westfield to St. John, and this road will only toe built from one point to another in order to suit people in certain parts of New Brunswick. I am soiry to have to make that statement. In 1912 it was contemplated that this road should be built as a through line from Grand Falls to St. John. Every local member along the 'St. John river advocated that policy. The provincial election has been carried on that policy, and we know the result. Now, we are told1 that they are not going to build the line, but that they are going to get a right of way for the St. John Valley Railway Company over the Canadian Pacific and the Intercolonial. We will have a kind of line that will be very unsatisfactory to the people of New Brunswick.
The Acting Minister of Railways has told us that the proposed arrangement of a terminus at Westfield, with running rights over the Canadian Pacific railway, was very fMr. Michaud.]
satisfactory to the people of St. John. I can tell him that the people of St. John are not so eas'ly satisfied. Not so very long ago the Premier of New Brunswick had a little trouble over this very line of railway, and his supporters had to whitewash his connection with the construction of this line. The people are far from satisfied with this arrangement, but they have to consent to it because they cannot get a better one under the circumstances.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. REID thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 98, to aid in the construction of certain lines of Tailway of the Saint John and Quebec Railway Company, and to confirm an agreement 'between the company and the Governments of Canada and New Brunswick.

I would suggest to the minister that a very good way of getting over the difficulty with regard to running rights would be to declare this work to be to the general advantage of Canada. It would then come under the Railway Act that was passed this session, and the Board of Railway Commissioners would have authority to grant the running rights. All that would be needed to bring the Bill under the Act would be to insert the words that the work was for the general advantage of Canada. Otherwise there might be some difficulty, because the company was incorporated by the Provincial Legislature and not by this Parliament.
I am glad of the suggestion, and will take it into consideration.

subtopic: MOUNT ROYAL TUNNEL AND TERMINAL COMPANY.
speechtext: As this is purely a legal matter perhaps I might venture to give a very short explanation. Under the Railway Act, the earnings of a company are to be applied towards certain objects in a definite order. The first application of the earnings is, I believe, towards fines, and the second, towards the payment of operating expenses.

subtopic: MOUNT ROYAL TUNNEL AND TERMINAL COMPANY.
speechtext:
Is this company a subsidiary of the Canadian Northern railway?
- Mr. MEIGHEN: Strictly speaking, it is, I think, a constituent company. While it is one of the companies that is part of the Canadian Northern Railway system, inasmuch as to a small extent it operates a line, it is a constituent company. The second application of the earnings of a company is towards operating expenses. After that, the applications are towards interest upon bond issues, and thereafter, towards payments of dividends on stock. The Mount Royal Tunnel and 'Terminal Company is a constituent company of the Canadian Northern Railway system. It.was constituted for the purpose of building the tunnel through Mount Royal, and 'for constructing the terminals at Montreal. In order to facilitate the financing-indeed, in order to make the financing possible-a separate company was formed, and its own bonds were issued. Consequently, they hope to he able to finance on those bonds, they being a first charge on the property of the company, and the property upon which they are a charge not being previously encumbered by all the charges against the Canadian Northern Railway itself. The rentals of the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company come from the Canadian Northern railway, from the Canadian Northern Ontario, and from the Canadian 213
Northern Quebec. In fact, all the properties of the company were to be utilized by these three companies-the parent company, the Canadian Northern Ontario, and the Canadian Northern Quebec. They paid the rentals for these properties in proportion to the use they obtained, and the revenues that were constituted by these rentals were to be the entire revenues of the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company. A bond issue was arranged for sufficient to provide for the building, and the rentals were fixed at a figure sufficient to meet the interest and the sinking fund upon the bond issue. However, in order to make the rentals certain, they were fixed . by the original Act of 1914 providing for the issue of these bonds and were made a charge against operation. Rentals are a charge against operation under the law generally, unless they go for the use of a line of railway, and inasmuch as the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company operated a short line, constituting, I believe, about 5 per cent of the enterprise, a special provision in the Act was necessary in order to make those rentals a charge against operation. Had they not operated any line at all the rentals would have been a charge against operation anyway. Consequently in this Act which this Parliament put through in 1914-1 do not refer to the main Act, chapter 20, statutes of 1914, but to the 'Tunnel Act, a private Act, that went through in that session-a clause was inserted providing that those rentals paid by these three companies, the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Northern Ontario, and the Canadian Northern Quebec, should constitute a charge against the operation of the three companies respectively. That made the security a very ample one and made it quite a relatively easy matter to finance the issue of bonds, and it was out of the issue of bonds that the whole institution secured its funds for prosecuting the work.
'Then a legal point arose later on, a point upon which there was difference of opinion. In fact, I think, at all events in numbers, the preponderance of opinion was that the Act, as it stood, had the effect that it is now desired to give to it by this legislation, but the solicitors for the bondholders took the ground, that owing to this Act of 1914 being in the nature of a private Act, it was not in its terms strong enough to overcome the general provision of the Railway Act, and that, although the section making those rentals a charge on operation had the effect of making them such as against any future



bond issue of those roads, it had not the effect of making them a charge as against prior bond issues of those roads. It was undoubtedly the intention of the statute that it should make them a charge on operating expenses against all bond issues.

Yes, this is the section. In this connection it would be eleaT if P read the section:
The whole of the rents or sums reserved or made payable under the said agreement or lease shall for all purposes he deemed to be, and are hereby declared to form part of the working expenditure, as defined and provided for in the Bailway Act, of the lessees parties to the said agreement or lease.
The contention was that the statute, namely, chapter 28 of the statutes of 1914, being in the nature of a private Act, the effect of this clause, which was in the statute, was not sufficient to make those rentals a charge against operating expenses as against prior bond issues of those three railways. It undoubtedly was the intention that they should be. It was contended, on the other hand, that the Act was not a private one at all; that although it was printed along with the private Acts, the Interpretation Act stated that no Act was a private Act unless it was stated to be a private Act, and that consequently this was not a private Act. However, the fact that the solicitors for the bond holders held to the contrary made the objection of a very practical character, and made it impossible to complete the sale of bonds. This legislation is for the purpose of making it clear that the section in the Act of 1914 was intended to have the effect of making those rentals a charge against the operating expenses of the three railways, even as against prior bondholders. Of course, it must be clear that no one's interests are interfered with by the legislation, because there has been no issue, and there will be no issue unless it is a charge. Consequently there are no prior rights interfered .with as yet. It is to make it clear that there never can be that this legislation is necessary.

speechtext: Is it not a question of our interfering with the prior rights of bondholders of the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Northern Ontario? It would not be the bondholders of the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company?

speechtext: No.

speechtext:
I have Tead the Bill over, and the only doubt that I have had -and it is not a very strong one undeT the circumstances-is as to whether we ought to pass legislation which might possibly interfere with the rights of third parties without their having an opportunity of being heard before the legislation is passed. If the Solicitor General is of the opinion that this does not in effect alter their rights, that, of course, would put it in a very different position. Then there is this to be borne in mind, that without the terminals at Montreal, the securities of the bondholders upon the Canadian Northern system would be very much impaired. No doubt it greatly improves the value of their security to have those terminals, and for those reasons I would be disposed to disregard what I thought at first would be a pretty strong objection to the legislation.
I am very strongly of the opinion that we should be very careful to safeguard any private rights and not interfere with them without hearing their side of the case.

subtopic: MOUNT ROYAL TUNNEL AND TERMINAL COMPANY.
speechtext: I remember the discussion that arose on this very point. The legal point is too fine for me to discuss, because I would get 'all tangled up in the technicalities if I tried to do so. As I understand it, however, this legislation is to make clear the intention of the Act of 1914. The question raised by my hon. friend from St. John is a very important one, and I presume that the Solicitor General has fully considered it. Leaving out the legal side of the case, I think it is very important that nothing at the present time should stand in the way of the company being able to dispose of its bonds for the carrying on of this work. As has been well said, the system is now incomplete and its earning power is retarded very much by the fact that the terminals at Montreal are not completed. Once they are completed, the earning power of the road will be very materially increased. To. those who are not conversant with the situation at Montreal, the necessity for the early completion of those terminals will be less apparent than they are to me, as I have been on the ground and have seen the slowness of the work. As I remember it, the intention of Parliament was to do. what this new legislation proposes now to make clear.

I was asking the attention of the minister to the nuisance caused in Montreal by the whistling of steamers using the Lachine canal. The canal goes
213J
through the city. It is crossed by many bridges. Many boats come down laden with grain or other cargo and the system is to give three long whistles on approaching a bridge-at least that seems to be the system so far as one can figure it out who lies long enough awake to hear what goes on. If he is not wakeful enough to follow the system, he will certainly be awak-. ened by some passing boat. This nuisance has become almost intolerable and some means should be found to put an end to it.

This is the first complaint on this subject that has come to my notice. Of course, I can understand that with so many boats using the canal the use of their whistles might become a nuisance. I will take thi6 matter up with the superintending engineer of the canal, Mr. Marceau, and inquire as to the facts and as to whether it is not possible to have the practice stopped, or, at least, made as little annoying as possible to residents. I suppose that a vessel approaching a bridge must blow a whistle as a signal.
It has been suggested that the signal should be given by means of a flashlight.
I am informed by the chief engineer that that has been considered, but the whistle is deemed the better signal in the interest of safety.
It is an awful nuisance to residents. A man, no matter how tired he may be at night, is kept awake by these long whistlings.

I understand that the difficulty is that a vessel coming round a curve cannot signal by flashlight which would be seen by the man at the lock or at the bridge. A vessel coming down the canal with the wind after her might find the bridge closed or the lock gates in the wrong position to receive her if she did not whistle.

The same argument was used some years ago when an attempt was made to prevent the whistling of locomotives in cities. Eventually this was stopped, and the railways have no difficulty in carrying on their business just as well without disturbing the whole city at night with their screeching whistles. Flash lights or signal lights could undoubtedly be used to notify the bridge keepers of the approach of vessels. This matter is well worthy of consideration by the department.
The bridge keepers could be notified by telephone that such and such a boat is on the way down; anything is better than the present system.

While it would be a good
thing for those living along the canal if this difficulty were removed, the main part of the city of Montreal is just east of the end of the canal, and the whistling of boats in the harbour would continue.

There is the difference
between the river and the canal that the river is a wide expanse of water and steamers are not numerous upon it. This canal is almost in the nature of a street, and the long shrills that are repeated by the vessels at every bridge are a standing nuisance.

When the minister takes this matter up he will have to deal with the Marine Association as well as with the Railway Department. The Marine Association, of course, has its own well defined rules and signals, and if vessels neglect to comply with them they are liable for any damages that may occur. Subject to that, I am of opinion that a good deal of the noise could be done away with on the canals.

That country is very
level, and once the railway is constructed, I understand that the iGovernment will have engineers on it for inspection purposes, to see that the work is carried out according to contract. There are a certain number of engineers necessary for sections. Perhaps the minister can give us the number of engineers that have been employed there. My information is that many more have been sent out than were necessary, and that when the Government wanted to give a man a job, or wanted to take a man from another job they sent him there.
I differ with the hon. gentleman. The chief engineer tells me that they have no more engineers on the staff than are actually necessary.

No. I cannot give the exact number of engineers at present. The hon. gentleman will see that we have spent on the railway, so far, $10,000,000; I have sufficient confidence in the chief engineer to believe that he would not put on more men than are necessary, and I have the same confidence in the Minister of Railways. He has tried to keep the staff down as low as possible.
With poor success.
Who is the engineer in charge?

There is a man named Porter in charge of the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. He is in Winnipeg. At Port Nelson there is a man named McLachlan. Mr. Porter has an assistant named Gordon.
Mr, GRAHAM: Is this the Mr. McLachlan who was formerly on the Trent canal?
That is the man.

I understand that the contractor operates it until it is taken over by tfie Government. He is operating it in a certain way.

Yes, right through to Port Nelson. .	<

We have a contract with J.

That estimate does not include the dredging of the channel. I am told you will have to dredge around the port.

We will have some dredging to do near the docks, but, I am informed, it will not he necessary to do any dredging out into Hudson 'bay. The dredging that will be necessary at the docks is included in the Estimate which I have given.
My hon. friend has not answered my question as to the number of engineers on that route. If he cannot give me the information at present, I would be glad if he would let me know later.

I understand from people who have been up there that dredging will be required out from the wharves into the bay itself and that the parts dredged will fill up again. I understood from one party who had been there that such a lot of silt comes down from the river that it will be impossible to keep the channel open without constant dredging, and that it will be like shuffling snow because as soon as one part is dredged it fills up again. Does the minister know anything about that? I got the information from a very responsible man who is not a partisan and who had been there and should have a knowledge of what is going on.
What is the tide theTe?

Sixteen feet is the ordinary spring tide. The only place necessary to dredge is out at the entrance. A channel from half a mile to fifteen miles wide, and with the depth I have stated, I think, should be satisfactory.
Does the minister expect to take large grain ships up a channel which has only twenty feet of water?
That is all the SL John harbour had until 1908.
But they have a very high tide at St. John.
This has a 16 feet tide and 19 and 16 would make 35 feet. That is the minimum, but that would be ample for Port Nelson.
What is the length of the channel from the dock to the bay?
About fifteen miles.
Will they go up the river fifteen miles?
The distance up the estuary from Hudson bay is fifteen miles.

There is a strong opinion in the minds of people down here that the channel from Port Nelson out to deep water in Hudson bay is rather narrow and crooked, that the silt brought down in the spring, and also after storms, changes the channel, and that if it is going to be navigable it will have to be continually dredged. One man who has been up there says that a vessel loaded with lumber for the department got stuck ten miles out from the harbour. I would like the minister to give us a pretty full explanation of the condition affecting this channel. I am not unduly criticising this project, because as a western man I want the route to be a success, but thousands of people in the East believe that the channel will be a very unsatisfactory one. I was glad to hear the minister state that the chief engineer says that there shall be a good wide channel. I would like to know if the channel can be depended upon year after year, or whether, if it has been dredged out one year it will fill up by next year.
Would the'hon. member care to take this map, showing the channel, and study it?

I have seen the map.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
I should like an answer to the questions I asked before six o'clock.

I have discussed the matter with the chief engineer and he tells me that the channel is quite safe, with a depth, of never less than 19 feet, and he assures me that my hon. friend need have no apprehension as to the sides falling in. The channel widens out from half a mile to 15 miles at the mouth, and there is a rise of 16 feet with the tide. I have here -the chart prepared, I think, by the officials of the Marine and Fisheries Department. These charts, of course, are never printed until a thorough examination has been made of the waters. The engineers engaged on this work prepare charts of the waters all over the Dominion; the charts are made with great care, and are very reliable. The hon. gentleman spoke of a vessel that was wrecked at the commencement of the work. As a matter of fact, two vessels were wrecked, one of which went ashore 14 miles out from the bay. At that time we did not have the aids to navigation we have now, but apart altogether from that, there was great carelessness on the part of those in charge of the vessel. Another vessel broke away after she had got safely into the harbour, and went ashore; but her cargo was saved. With the exception of these two accidents, which we attribute to carelessness, vessels have been navigating these .waters continually since the work commenced, in perfect safety. The three steamers which the Government purchased have been operated each year between the lower provinces and Port Nelson, carrying as cargo the material required in the carrying on of the work. Several vessels have also been chartered, and since the commencement of the work, with the exception of the two cases I have mentioned, there have been no mishaps, or practically none. I think my hon. friend, after seeing the chart, which I will now lay on the Table, will agree that the channel is safe, and feel justified in contradicting any rumours to the contrary he may hear in the future.

The minister has said that the estimated cost of the harbour improvements will be $10,000,000. Has the depart-xnent a plan, showing what these harbour
improvements are, their nature and extent, and what purpose they are to serve? If the harbour as it stands to-day is a good harbour, $10,000,000 seems a lot of money to spend on it.
I would like the hon. member for Assiniboia to have a look at this chart.
In case of a storm on the bay vessels could net reach the harbour for safetv
Where the 30 feet of water is, there are mud flats on each side, and these would be a protection if the tide were out.
If 'a storm arose and if the tide was out, the vessel would have to ride out the storm the best way she could.

Not if she got in between the mud flats, where she would have thirty feet of water. Tin greatest wave is three feet over the mud Hats, so that she would be pretty safe from tny storm. The channel is very wide; as you go out it extends to fifteen miles wide; that is, with the depth of water that I have stated.
If the channel is fifteen miles wide and there is no shelter, there is certainly room to raise a tremendous sea.

The channel starts at about half a mile wide, and as you go out, it extends to about fifteen miles wide; but you can get in close to the mud flats on each side, and the chief engineer says that three feet is the highest wave they have had with the great storms up in that section; so that a vessel drawing not more than nineteen feet of water can get far enough up the river to be out of any great danger in a storm.

My knowledge of navigation is not sufficient to enable me to argue the point. What I have ini mind in discussing the matter is, that the port of Churchill is a shelter harbour, a harbour to which vessels may safely go in .storms. There is deep water there, and there is not the enormous expenditure required in order to make the handling of traffic possible. What I am interested in is: What is the advantage claimed for the use of this port of Nelson, which has certain disadvantages, as against the port of Churchill which has certain obvious and unquestioned advantages? I know there is a difference in the train haul, that it is somewhat further to Churchill than to Nelson; but it

appears to me that the difference in the train haul does not anything like compensate for the difference in the advantage of having a deep water shelter harbour as at Churchill, as compared with a very questionable proposition such as exists at Nelson, because no vessel owner is going to risk his vessel on a route where the harbour accommodation is at all questionable. Every one knows that when a vessel gets near land, the shipmaster becomes afraid, and when the port is not of such a character as to lend itself to the safety and advantage of shipping, the shipping keeps away from it. That is a handicap that Nelson will necessarily have to overcome. I want to know why Nelson was chosen in place of Churchill.

I suppose the Minister of
Railways and Canals would probably be better able to answer that than I; but so far as Nelson and Churchill are concerned, there is eighty miles difference in the length of railway which would mean that, if Churchill were chosen, you would have to haul a train 160 miles further each return journey. That, of course, means a large expense in connection with a railway system; it means one division more, and that would be a good reason for choosing Port Nelson, everything else being equal.
I understand that while Churchill is a good harbour, there is not the same anchorage for vessels as there is a Port Nelson, that is for a large traffic. The terminal question has been' already discussed. The Minister of Railways sent an engineer to look over the situation in order to see whether Churchill or vNelson would be the more suitable, and the reports received by him were that Port Nelson had certain advantages, one of which I have mentioned, that it was a good harbour, and that the channel and so on were quite satisfactory. In addition to that, the minister himself made a trip to Port Nelson and also to Churchill to look after the situation; other officials of the department also examined the different places, and it was after giving the matter every consideration that Port Nelson was finally decided upon. However, rightly or wrongly, the matter has been definitely decided upon and the work has gone on to such an extent that we could not change the port now, and I do not know that there is much use in going further into the matter on that account.

I am not very clear as to what the minister means in regard to the shelter for ships. From the map, I 
would think that it is an exposed harbour and that a gale blowing from the northeast or somewhat in that direction would blow right into that harbour. So far as I can see, the fact of a mud bank being on each side of the channel would not be of any assistance. A breakwater would be of value and I believe that before the minister gets through with this harbour, he will have to build one. I suppose he is aware that when a ship comes in from a long voyage, it is usual to let the steam go down and to fix up the grates and get her ready for the next voyage; but ships lying in an exposed place like that would require to keep steam up in order to be safe in case a gale came up suddenly; otherwise, they might be driven on the flats. The harbour itself does not look as if there were much shelter. I am not clear as to the fact of its being narrow. Is there any bend in the river or any protection from the wind that gives the ships any shelter at that point?

If the hon. gentleman will
look at the chart, he will see that there are mud flats on each side. If a northeast gale came right up the channel, the waves on each side of the channel would still be very small, because it is so shallow, and there would not be such a storm in the channel as there would be out in the ocean. The hon. member knows that the tide rises and falls twice a day and it would be only a very short time before a vessel could get right on to the pier that we are building; she would hot have to lie out in the channel for any length of time in an exposed position even if a storm arose.

Is there good shelter
at the pier?

Right at the pier she would be out of the storm altogether, because the land is on each side. I take it for granted that the hon. member is speaking about eight or nine miles from the pier that we are constructing for the vessels to tie up at.

There is no doubt that this Hudson Bay route is viewed with a measure of suspicion by a large proportion of the people of Canada. They have doubts as to the wisdom of the expenditure of money on the railroad because they have no faith in the navigation of the bay. There is no doubt that, looked at from a railroad point of view, the port of Nelson is the better port, tout looked at from the point of view of the navigator or shipowner, unless it is an advantageous port, then all

the expenditure that is being made is thrown away and the project is discredited. It is a matter of supreme importance that the port shall be of such a character as will attract shipping and not tend to drive it elsewhere. Having beyond any question such a port at Churchill, although the rail haul would be eighty miles further, the cost of construction, at the same rate as the road is now costing, of that eighty miles, would be less than $3,000,000, whereas the improvements at the port of Nelson are going to cost $10,000,000 and may cost a great deal more than that. The point I want to make is that all this expenditure is not properly chargeable to the Hudson Bay railway and Hudson Bay route proposition. $18,000,000 would carry the railroad to Churchill and a moderate expenditure at the port of Churchill would give the necessary facilities for handling traffic at that port. There would be no question then in the minds of shipowners as to the advantage of the route, and once traffic had been established by that route, then, if business increased, you would have the time and occasion to develop the port of Nelson; but at the present time, as it appears to me, we are risking the expenditure we are making and the prospect turning out to be a success, in the effort to create a port where no port now exists. I have taken the liberty of putting this view of the case before the Minister of Railways on previous occasions, and until we are shown, by plans and specifications laid on the table of the House, a well conceived proposal for the development of an adequate and satisfactory port at Nelson, I feel that I am compelled to keep before the public the idea that the Hudson Bay route is not getting a fair chance when Nelson is being used instead of Churchill. It may be that the Government will spend enough money on Nelson to make it a suitable port, but the success of t'he route depends upon the possibility of port Nelson being made satisfactory to the shipping interests. It may easily be that while that can be done, it may cost too much money to do it, and unless it is done, the route is necessarily discredited. My hon. friend has said that there is no use in discussing the relative merits of Churchill and Nelson with a view to abandoning Nelson and adopting Churchill. Possibly that is true, but my effort is to impress upon the Government that, having selected Nelson to be the terminus of the railroad, they have taken upon themselves the responsibility of seeing that
project through and seeing that Nelson is made a port satisfactory to the shipping interests, and that the Government which chose the port of Nelson instead of the port of Churchill must take the full responsibility for that choice, for whatever expenditure is necessary and for whatever success or failure is attained. They must not lay the burden upon the Hudson project or route, they must take the burden upon their own shoulders. If they succeed, we will certainly all give them credit and we will all be glad; but if they do not succeed, the blame must rest upon themselves and not upon the project of a Hudson bay railway and route.

The hon. member is absolutely correct when he states thdt the harbour and entrances must be made suitable for shipowners. Any government would have to make them satisfactory to the shipowners, and that is being done up to the present time. Every shipowner who has sent his vessel to Nelson has been well satisfied with the charts that we have at the present time. Up to the present the expenditure made at Port Nelson would be the same as would have to be made at Churchill, because it covers, in a very large measure, the plant that we would have to have for Churchill. Previous to the Minister of Railways taking charge of the department, the whole Hudson bay project was investigated and decided upon by the late Administration, and it ^ras a project that was put forward with the consent of both parties, in the interest of the West. Even if Port Nelson were to cost more money at the present time and be as suitable as Fort Churchill, I claim that it would be much better to spend that money at Port Nelson than at Fort Churchill for the reason that if we had chosen Fort Churchill which the hon. member is now advocating, we would have to haul each trainload of wheat produced in the Northwest eighty miles further to put into a vessel, and we would have to haul that train back the same eighty miles. It costs money to do that and who is going to pay for the 160 miles haulage of that train? Surely the hon. member knows that the additional cost of operation would have to be borne by the farmers in the West in the form of an increased freight rate. Does not the hon. member agree with me that if we can get a port where we can save that 160 miles haulage for all time to come, the amount that would be saved in a few years would pay probably twice as much as the whole cost of the terminus? I do not think there can be any difference of opinion on that.

The hon. member is under the impression that the Minister of Railways and Canals, from information given by his officials and any evidence that he could get, thought that development of Port Nelson would cost a great deal more than would Churchill; and the hon. member for Edmonton is of the same opinion. The Minister of Railways and Canals was to decide which of the two harbours would be of most advantage to the farmers of the Northwest, and which would cost the least money. The opinion that he had up to that time was that to build a railway to Churchill would mean an additional haul of 80 miles each way; that was one thing against it. The information that the Minister of Railways and Canals had before him at that time as to the cost of the work necessary to put the harbour at Churchill in satisfactory condition was as follows: harbour work, piers, dredging, exclusive of lighthouse and buoying, $6,675,000. The cost of the same work at. Port Nelson, covering exactly the same items, was estimated at $5,065,000. I do not know whether it was the opinion of the hon. member for South Renfrew himself; at all events it was the opinion of the officials, that Port Nelson was a safe and a good harbour; that the selection of that port would save a haul of 80 miles which would have been a charge on the farmers of the Northwest for all time to come had the other port been selected. Every farmer who had grain to send could save half a cent a bushel on the carriage of that grain if it went through Port Nelson instead of Churchill, and, besides, the difference in the cost of the works at the respective harbours would be $1,600,000.
Who made that report? [DOT]

.I was just reading from a report on the Hudson Bay railway, made by Mr. Armstrong in 1909, and revised by Mr. Butler. In connection with cost over and above the amount mentioned, it should be remembered that all the plant is now a charge on these terminals. The officials of the department, from the deputy minister down to every man who was sent there, did their best to get the most accurate figures. From the information I have I believe that Mr. Butler, the deputy minister at the time; Mr. Armstrong, the engineer in charge, and all his officials, came to the conclusion, from the information they could get, that Port Nelson was the right place. Mr. Cochrane sent another man there, and his report was exactly the

same. Then Mr. Cochrane himself went there and examined the place, and he came to the same conclusion. Under the circumstances I do not see that any fault can be found with the decision that has been arrived at. The captains who have navigated ships there believe that Port Nelson is the right place.
The minister said that ship owners who sent ships there were quite satisfied with Port Nelson. For what purposes were these ships sent there?
We have 'been running our own vessels with supplies, but prior to our obtaining these we had to charter vessels.

I thought the minister meant ships that sent there for commercial purposes. The men that the department sent there would be satisfied because they were getting a high price for the use of their vessels. Has any report -been received from men engaged in the transportation business in Hudson bay?
I would like to ask hon. gentlemen in this House if, since this Hudson Bay railway project was commenced, anyone could do more than has been done by the present minister and his two predecessors?
It was all done by railway men.

It was all done by officials of the department, and they got the best evidence they, could. Vessels of the Marine Department have been going there, and many vessels have been chartered and sent to Port Nelson with full cargoes of supplies.
How many of them have been lost?

One was lost 14 miles away from the channel; she had got altogether out of her course. The other vessel that was lost got into port, -but through carelessness she was allowed to drift from her anchorage to the shore. Afterwards they supposed that she had been set fire to. The minister in. deciding which shall be the terminal port can only take the -best evidence that he can get. He sends his engineers to look the ports over; they examine them to the best of their ability; he gets what information he can from vessels that have been in the locality. When a minister comes to a decision under these circumstances, taking the advice of hie

deputy minister, his engineers, and considering all available information, even if it should turn out afterwards to be wrong, I claim that he has done his duty. I believe that all available information was exhausted by the present minister's predecessors in determining what port would he the best, having regard to the interests of the people of the Northwest, and I believe that the same has been the case with the present minister. The port has been decided upon, and I sincerely hope that the anticipations of everyone who has had anything to do with this decision will turn out to be wgll founded. We hope also that the Tailway will be a success. I stated in this House a few days ago that at first, many years ago, I was under the impression that this railroad would not 'be the success it is now expected to he, but I have changed my opinion, and I think many other would, if they had the same opportunity as I have had of discussing this matter with, the officers who know the whole situation, with those who have been up there, with captains who have navigated the bay, and of hearing from the Minister of Railways and Canals his opinion of what can be done. I believe now that when we get that road in operation, the Northwest will receive benefits which some of us at the present time can hardly conceive.

The minister knows that I have always favoured the construction of the Hudson Bay railway, but I must say that I had always expected that Fort Churchill would be the terminus of that road. That idea is in conformity with the information which we in the Maritime Provinces gather from old seamen who have navigated Hudson bay, and from the owners of vessels who had traded there. They always expected that when the railload was constructed, Fort Churchill would be the natural port, beeause there you have a natural harbour, and the conditions are safer. They looked upon Port Nelson as a problem which might never be solved. The minister said that it would have been necessary to construct .some 80 miles of railway additional, if Fort Churchill had been selected as the terminus, hut I am not sure that a line further west might not have been .selected which could have reached Fort Churchill without necessitating the construction of the extra 80 miles of road. If the conditions are more favourable at Fort Churchill, as is stated by the old seamen who have navigated Hudson
bay, that extra expense would have been compensated for by the better navigation facilities, 'by lower insurance rates, and so on. At any ralte, the opinion of these men is that Fort Churchill would have been more advantageous than Port Nelson. Meanwhile, the minister tells us that it is too late to think of Fort Churchill. I do noit blame ithe minister. He must have taken the best advice he could get, and no doubt it was given to him honestly, but it does not agree with the general opinion of the seamen in the Maritime Provinces. If the decision is irrevocable, I would urge upon the minister the necessity of improving the harbour at Port Nelson at any cost, so that it will render the services for which the Hudson Bay railway is being constructed. I have not unlimited faith in the period of navigation. It is limited to a period of three months in the year, but three months in the year for the West, with the development which we may expect, would be of great advantage to the grain shippers and to those engaged in cattle raising. It would give a new impetus to development in the Northwest, and enable the farmers to ship at a greater advantage than they can with the long haul to our eastern seaboard. I would strongly urge upon the minister the necessity of improving that harbour. But the decision arrived at by the department is altogether contrary to the opinion expressed by men from St. John's, Newfoundland, and by other men who have navigated Hudson bay, and who have no political interest in the matter at all. I wish to impress the minister with that fact.

What became of the
dredge that was shipped up there? It was said that it had been broken up and was useless. I think it was shipped from Toronto. Is it in use now? While I am on my feet, might I ask if there are any reports from the men engaged in constructing the railway as to the prospect of western freight, as well as eastern freight, along the railway, or adjacent to it.
The dredge referred to worked for about nine weeks last year, and it has been working since with perfect satisfaction.

Something went wrong
with it when it first went up there. .

Yes, it was damaged when
it was beached for the winter,' but it has

been repaired. It gave good satisfaction for nine weeks, and will do good work during the coming season. With regard to freight going west, that is a hard matter to decide. We all have our own opinions as to that. I am under the impression that there will be cargoes from the Hudson Bay. There will be cargoes of grain going direct to foreign countries-
That would be eastbound freight. Is there any prospect of westbound freight?
There are coal, steel rails, and other products that will go West, and there is the possibility of freights from Montreal and the lower provinces.
I do not mean that; I mean local freight along the length of the railway, between Hudson bay and the Pas.

Along the railway there is timber, and fish, and minerals. I noticed that they were getting minerals along that line, and I am informed that there is good agricultural country. The information I have is that there is a. great quantity of timber and minerals, and of course there are fish.
The timber is not worth very much according to the report.
For local consumption it is.

In the topographical
survey report for 1916, a good deal of the timber is described as pretty scrubby, and a good deal of the land is described as muskeg. There is said to be some clay land fit for cultivation, but a great deal of it is swampy. The report says there are some whitefish and trout in the locality and that only a small amount of tillable land is found in the district covered by forest. Fishing and mining are likely to prove, the report states, most important industries. There is also a paragraph in the report which says that frost occurs every month of the year, excepting perhaps July, and that at the beginning of May, 1914, there were two feet of snow, *which had not entirely disappeared before the middle of June, and the frosty nights began on August 20. So that it is a pretty rigorous climate in which to expect any agricultural settlement. According to this report, there are strips of timber on the banks of the rivers, and some clay land, but a good deal of it is swampy, and apparently the climate is very cold.

As far as frost is concerned, last summer we had the largest and best crop we have ever had in the West, in Saskatchewan at all events, and there was frost in every month during the year 1915 without a single exception. It does not necessarily follow that because there may be some frost during each month it will not be a good agricultural country. As my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) says, they raise very fine vegetables in the Yukon. There is a large tract of good clay land for agricultural purposes in the Burnt river country. Irrespective of the merits of the road as a through route, it will be a good colonization road and there will be a considerable amount of settlement going in! on a part of the line at all events. No doubt for mixed farming it will be found suitable.

I wish to say a word or two with regard to that question of temperature. I have made a considerable study of the Hudson bay route and I have got the best information I could upon the subject. I do not think it is necessary for me to go back over the ground to-day. I do not wish to accuse the East of any prejudice but if the people in this part of the country will just look' squarely at the conditions in the West there will not be one word of opposition to the building of the Hudson Bay route or of doubt with respect to the navigability of Hudson bay and Hudson straits. What I rose to reply to was the question to which my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) referred about there being frost in every month of the year except one. My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has answered that. In the three provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba there was not one month last year in which we did not have frost. Further than that, in a year when we had one of the best crops that we ever had, we had seven or eight inches of snow on the 12th June and another snowstorm on the 15th September. That. is such a wonderful country that all these little obstacles do not interfere with us having good crops, nor will they interfere with transportation out of that country by way of Hudson bay and Hudson strait. It is not necessary at this late day to give proof of the great necessity there is for an outlet from the West such as that road will afford. I want to draw the attention of the House to one or two points. One has reference to the matter of growing wheat. Some people tell us that we can grow apples and fruit in the West. I have an experience since 1882

and my opinion is that while we may grow fruit, the staple articles that the farmer will grow in that country for many years, will he grain and stock. Wheat has commanded a very good price, and at the price that wheat sells for to-day we can afford, perhaps, to send our wheat over this long 'haul to Montreal and make it pay. I may *be too pessimistic about this
9 p.m. matter, but when you consider the tremendous amount of wheat and other grain that has to be handled you will see how important the transportation question becomes. When you consider that we have at least 126,000,000 acres that can produce grain, that today we only have about 20,000,000 under cultivation, and that this year we grew some 600,000,000 bushels of grain, it gives you some idea of what that country is going to produce. When our production increases and when that of all the other grain-growing countries in the world, now. producing enormous quantities, increases, wheat will not naturally be at the price at which it sells to-day. Then we in this Parliament- and I do not care which Government is in control-will have to do our utmost to lighten the cost of transportation, whether by the railways or by the Hudson bay route. I do not need to point out to the committee the great difference there is between the cost of transportation by water and by land. It is much cheaper by water. I do not need to tell you that while in Manitoba we may get along, if you have to provide for t'he production of Alberta and the Peace river district, which everybody says will grow any amount of grain, the problem becomes still more pressing. I am going to give the figures to the committee to show the difference in the cost of getting wheat out by way of Hudson bay and bringing it down to Montreal. This is not the first railway that 'has met with opposition. This is not the first time that we have heard about a frozen up country. I will guarantee that when my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) went out to that country he got his life insured for fear 'he would be killed by Indians, or that he would freeze to death and never reach civilization again. I know that to be a fact.
Oh, oh.
Not as to the details.

That is the way they talk about this country. There is no question to-day as to the navigability of Hudson bay and Hudson strait. My 'hon. friend from Guysboro (Mr. Sinclair), who comes from near Halifax, talks about the temperature, but let me tell him that the average from the Ilth July until October is 62i degrees. That mean average temperature for these four months is better than that of ten of the principal stations extending from Halifax, N.S., to Fort 'Simpson, on the Mackenzie river.
He does not live near Halifax.

Yes, he lives pretty near Halifax. About two-thirds of the southern part of Hudson bay may be considered to have had that temperature. The United States went through this same thing. They felt just the same as some of our eastern friends feel now-if they do feel that way-and I am afraid, from the little private conversations I have had outside, that some of the eastern people think that this is going to interfere with their business. I have every assurance in so far as I am personally concerned, and I am not an engineer, but I am just as good an engineer as many hon. gentlemen on the other side who talk about this route, that Hudson bay and Hudson strait are navigable for five months in the year. It is a very peculiar fact that no iceberg ever appears in Hudson bay, and no iceberg ever appears in the first 400 miles of Hudson strait. The only icebergs we have in that country come from near my hon. friend's country; they form off the Newfoundland coast, come up the Hudson strait about 100 miles, until the current sets in the other way and they are carried out to sea. It is a fact that there never was an iceberg found in Hudson bay or Hudson strait for the first 400 miles. There was similar opposition and criticism in the United States when the port of Galveston was opened; it was said that the Eastern States would be ruined. But what was the result? Instead of ruining the Eastern States, the opening of that port has been of great advantage to them, because it has given it has given them a tremendous market for their manufactured products.
I do not think anybody " here ds afraid that eastern Canada will be hurt.

Why is there always so much opposition then? But I do not wish to dwell on that. Western Canada must have a road to Hudson Bay. With proper aids to

navigation I believe that Hudson Bay will be navigable but if not, it will be a serious thing for western Canada. I should like to give the House a few figures showing the comparative distances from Liverpool, and I think they will be somewhat of a surprise to a great many members. From Fort Churchill to Liverpool is 3,000 miles; from Montreal to Liverpool is 3,220. I am dealing with Fort Churchill because I have always been and still am of the opinion-I am always open to conviction-that Fort Churchill was the place to choose. I am not an engineer, and the engineers may have been able to prove that Port Nelson was more advantageous. But I have to agree occasionally with the hon. member for Edmonton.
It hurts, eh?

If Fort Churchill is the better port, and engineers say it is, then to my mind the difference of 80 miles of railway is not a strong argument for changing from Fort Churchill to Port Nelson. I am rather of the impression that hon. member for South Renfrew talked of making this change when the late Government was in power. I may be wrong, but I think my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) was in favour of Port Nelson rather than Fort Churchill. From Montreal to Liverpool is 220 miles more than from Fort Churchill to Liverpool. The distance from New York to Liverpool is 3,057 miles. From St. Paul to Liverpool via New York 4,440 miles; from St. Paul to Liverpool via Hudson bay 4,096 miles. From Duluth via New York to Liverpool, 4,201 miles; from Duluth via Hudson bay to Liverpool, 3,728 miles. From Vancouver to Liverpool via Canadian Pacific railway is 5,868 miles; from Vancouver to Liverpool via Hudson bay 4,568 miles. The Hudson bay route means a saving between Vancouver and Liverpool of 1,300 miles, which ought to mean something. Now let us take the land distances. From Brandon to Montreal the distance is 1,555 miles; from Brandon to Churchill 940 miles; from Medicine Hat to Montreal 2,082 miles; from Medicine Hat to Churchill 1,0716 miles; from Calgary to Churchill is 1,256 miles; from Calgary to Montreal 2,262 miles; from Winnipeg to Montreal 1,422 miles; and from Winnipeg to Churchill 945 miles.
By what route?

By any route, Canadian Northern railway or Canadian Pacific railway. From Prince Albert to Montreal the distance is 1,958 miles; from Prince Albert to Churchill 717 miles. From Battle-
[Mr. Schaffner.J
ford to Montreal 1,094 miles; from Battle-ford to ChuTchill 876 miles. From Saskatoon to Montreal 1924 miles; from Saskatoon to Churchill 806 miles. From Edmonton to Montreal 2,247 miles; and from Edmonton to Churchill 1,129 miles. These figures have all been verified and can be taken as correct. They show conclusively how much shorter a land haul the Hudson Bay route means without entailing any greater distance by water. I am not going into this question to-night as fully as I have done in the past. I am personally convinced that the Lord placed Hudson bay where it is, to help out that great western country, and we do' not want His followers in the East to try and obstruct Him. I believe that route will be a God-send to the people of the West. We have only to turn to history to see how every enterprise has been opposed. Everybody knows what was said about the Canadian Pacific railway; but no enterprise under the sun has proved a greater success. People talked the same way about the Panama Canal.
The Transcontinental will turn out the same.

I believe it will some years hence; and since the hon. gentleman has brought up that point I will state my position. There is plenty of work for the Canadian Northern railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Canadian Pacific railway across the three Prairie Provinces. I do not think we should have had three roads built from Port Arthur east, at all events further east than Sudbury or North Bay. I am also of the opinion that there is not at the present time business for three roads west of Edmonton. But I have every confidence in my country, and I believe the time will come when those roads will all be in successful operation. This country is going to grow, and will have plenty of work for the three roads, and plenty of work for the Hudson Bay road also. I have figures for the last fifty years showing for how many months in the year the bay and straits are navigable. Without giving the figures for each year, the average time during which the bay and straits are navigable is from June 19 to November 8. I have no doubt that when we have all possible aids to navigation, the bay and straits will be navigable for from four to five months; and if we get four months during which the bay and straits are navigable it will be of the utmost

benefit to the country. I am not a prophet, but I should like my words here to-night to be remembered: It will not be very many years, perhaps within ten, when whoever is lucky enough to have a seat in this House will be wondering how any one ever had the courage to stand up in the face of Nature and say a single word against the building of the HudSon Bay railway and the navigability of Hudson bay and straits.

The last remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Schaffner), it seems to me, prove that as a grain-carrying route the Hudson Bay route will be good for only about one month in the year. He has. told us that the experience of some thirty years showed that the .season was from 19th June to 8th November. Now, I would submit this question to the judgment of the hon. gentleman: Who is going to send grain to Hudson bay after the 8th of November and run the risk of carrying that grain until June, at a time when the crops from the , southern countries are coming into the markets of the world, and when, as everybody in the business knows, grain begins to get a little cheaper? The only profitable carrying month for grain by the Hudson Bay route will be from the time when the grain starts to move-and it does not begin to move until about October-until the 8th of November. I am not going to debate the advantages and disadvantages of the Hudson Bay route, but it does seem to me that, at this time, when Canada has such great need of money, the Hudson Bay route could well wait for a little while. Let it wait until we have demonstrated that the .West can produce year after year such crops as it produced last year. It must be remembered that last year's was a phenomenal crop. For many years- before that we had but a limited crop. There is one feature of this argument that appears as a perennial problem to me. For about half the session our western friends put up the argument in favour of opening the markets of the United States, and for the other half they say they want the grain to go North for export. I want to know which is right. Who is going to send grain for storage at Hudson bay, pay freight and banking charges, insurance and storage, from November until June, keeping it there until the wheat of next year's crop begins to come in?

I thought I made that very clear. We can afford to sell our wheat a great deal cheaper when we send it by
the Hudson Bay route than when we send it by Montreal, because it will not cost us nearly so much to get it to market.

It may be expected that I should say a word or two upon the subject. I am not sure of the correctness of those distances given by the minister. Is the minister sure that from Pas Mission to Nelson is 425 miles?
That is in the printed report.

My recollection is that
the distance is 410 miles, but I may be wrong.

report, but I have it in the memorandum given me by the deputy minister. I may just read the information it contains.
